--- course-unit: ch08-agent-based-models status: complete --- # Agent-based models {#sec-agent-based-models} ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 3, Session 2. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd). ::: An agent-based model (ABM) represents a population as interacting individuals. The SIR labels remain familiar, but the model can now make explicit who contacts whom, when an agent changes status, and how an update schedule can affect results. This chapter uses a small, well-mixed ABM so that the connection to the population equations stays visible. ## Learning goals You will: - classify an individual-level SIR model and distinguish it from a count model; - implement a synchronous contact-and-recovery rule with Agents.jl 7; - collect model-level data with the current `StandardABM` and `run!` APIs; and - compare an ensemble of individual simulations with the deterministic SIR ODE while identifying effects that aggregation hides. ## Model assumptions and classification The population has $N=1000$ named individuals. Initially 10 are infectious, 990 are susceptible, and none are recovered. At every $\Delta t=0.1$ time unit, a susceptible makes $K\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(c\Delta t)$ random contacts. A contact chooses a uniformly random individual and transmits with probability $\beta$ if that individual is infectious. An infectious agent recovers with probability $1-\exp(-\gamma\Delta t)$. Recovered agents are immune. We use $c=10$, $\beta=0.05$, and $\gamma=0.25$. This is a **stochastic, discrete-time, discrete-state, individual-level** model. Time is discrete because `StandardABM` advances in integer steps; state is discrete because each `Person.status` is one of `:S`, `:I`, or `:R`. The population is well mixed because the model has no spatial structure: `StandardABM(Person)` uses the `nothing` space. This is an ABM even though its aggregated contact rule is designed to approximate mass action. ## Equations Let $Z_i(t)\in\{S,I,R\}$ be individual $i$'s status and $I_t=\sum_i\mathbf{1}(Z_i(t)=I)$. For a susceptible, the probability of no successful transmission in one step, conditional on $K_i=k$, is $$ \left(1-\beta\frac{I_t}{N}\right)^k. $$ Averaging over $K_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(c\Delta t)$ gives $$ \Pr(Z_i(t+\Delta t)=I\mid Z_i(t)=S) =1-\exp\!\left[-c\Delta t\,\beta\frac{I_t}{N}\right]. $$ {#eq-abm-infection} The recovery probability is $$ \Pr(Z_i(t+\Delta t)=R\mid Z_i(t)=I)=1-\exp(-\gamma\Delta t). $$ For small $\Delta t$, Equation @eq-abm-infection is approximately $\beta c(I_t/N)\Delta t$, matching the SIR force of infection. The individual model still carries more state than the population equations: each agent's current status is retained, so the population counts are a summary we choose to compute rather than the model's only representation. Contacts and potential transmission sources exist during an update but are not logged by this implementation; recording who infected whom would require an event history or extra agent fields. The ODE only tracks the totals and uses the deterministic flow $$ \dot S=-\beta cSI/N,\qquad \dot I=\beta cSI/N-\gamma I,\qquad \dot R=\gamma I. $$ ## Julia implementation Agents.jl 7 requires the `@agent` macro for supported agent types. In the installed 7.0.3 API, `NoSpaceAgent` contributes the mandatory `id` field; `StandardABM(Person; agent_step!, model_step!, properties, rng)` constructs a discrete-time model. We use a two-phase update: `agent_step!` reads the old statuses and writes `next_status`, then `model_step!` commits all changes. Without this separation, activation order could let a newly infected agent transmit in the same step. ::: {#code-ch06-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Agents using CairoMakie using Distributions using OrdinaryDiffEq using StableRNGs using Statistics const N = 1000 const I₀ = 10 const β = 0.05 const c = 10.0 const γ = 0.25 const Δt = 0.1 const nsteps = 300 const times = collect(0.0:Δt:(nsteps * Δt)) @agent struct Person(NoSpaceAgent) status::Symbol next_status::Symbol end ``` ::: The contact loop uses the model's random-number generator through `abmrng(model)`. `random_agent(model)` is the current Agents.jl helper for uniformly selecting an agent from a no-space model. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-rules .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function agent_step!(person, model) person.next_status = person.status if person.status == :S for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt)) contact = random_agent(model) if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β person.next_status = :I break end end elseif person.status == :I if rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt) person.next_status = :R end end return nothing end function model_step!(model) for person in allagents(model) person.status = person.next_status end return nothing end susceptible_count(model) = count(person.status == :S for person in allagents(model)) infected_count(model) = count(person.status == :I for person in allagents(model)) recovered_count(model) = count(person.status == :R for person in allagents(model)) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-rules .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` recovered_count (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: The model properties are a named tuple, so `model.β`, `model.c`, and `model.Δt` are ordinary Julia field accesses. The `mdata` functions below are called by `run!` at the initial state and after each step. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-constructor .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function initialize_model(seed) model = StandardABM( Person; agent_step!, model_step!, properties = (β = β, c = c, γ = γ, Δt = Δt), rng = StableRNG(seed), ) for id in 1:N status = id <= I₀ ? :I : :S add_agent!(Person(; id, status, next_status = status), model) end return model end model = initialize_model(20250711) agent_data, model_data = run!( model, nsteps; mdata = [susceptible_count, infected_count, recovered_count], showprogress = false, ) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-constructor .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: `run!` returns two data frames: one for agent observations and one for model observations. We requested only model-level totals, which keeps the example small while retaining the full individual state inside the model. The first row is the initial condition because `init=true` is the default. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-ode .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} abm_states = Matrix(model_data[:, [ :susceptible_count, :infected_count, :recovered_count, ]])' abm_times = Float64.(model_data.time) .* Δt function sir_drift!(du, u, p, t) β, c, γ, N = p infection = β * c * u[1] * u[2] / N du[1] = -infection du[2] = infection - γ * u[2] du[3] = γ * u[2] return nothing end ode_problem = ODEProblem( sir_drift!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, nsteps * Δt), (β, c, γ, N), ) ode_solution = solve(ode_problem, Tsit5(); saveat = abm_times) ode_states = Array(ode_solution) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-ode .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3×301 Matrix{Float64}: 990.0 989.499 988.986 988.46 … 247.327 246.6 245.886 10.0 10.2479 10.5017 10.7615 59.1809 58.4369 57.7002 0.0 0.253087 0.512444 0.77822 693.492 694.963 696.414 ``` ::: ::: The model time reported by a discrete `StandardABM` is the step number, so the explicit multiplication by $\Delta t$ maps it to the physical time used by the ODE. ::: {#cell-fig-ch06-abm .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (760, 430)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "people", title = "Well-mixed individual-based SIR") for (j, (name, color)) in enumerate(zip(["S", "I", "R"], [:steelblue, :firebrick, :seagreen])) stairs!(ax, abm_times, abm_states[j, :]; color, linewidth = 2, label = "$name (ABM)") lines!(ax, abm_times, ode_states[j, :]; color, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 1.5, label = "$name (ODE)") end axislegend(ax, position = :rt, nbanks = 2) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch06-abm .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` One individual-based SIR realization and the corresponding ODE trajectory. ::: ::: ## Validation The ABM has an exact bookkeeping invariant: every person has exactly one status. Consequently $S+I+R=N$ at every recorded step. The status graph is also one-way ($S\to I\to R$, with no return), so $S$ can never increase and $R$ can never decrease. Checking the recorded initial row as well confirms that `run!` collected the initial condition rather than the state after one step. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-validation .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} population_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(abm_states; dims = 1)) .- N)) @assert population_error == 0 @assert minimum(abm_states) >= 0 @assert abm_states[:, 1] == [N - I₀, I₀, 0] @assert all(diff(abm_states[1, :]) .<= 0) @assert all(diff(abm_states[3, :]) .>= 0) (; population_error, initial_counts = abm_states[:, 1], final_counts = abm_states[:, end], peak_abm = maximum(abm_states[2, :]), peak_ode = round(maximum(ode_states[2, :]); digits = 1), largest_gap = round(Int, maximum(abs.(abm_states[2, :] .- ode_states[2, :])))) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-validation .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (population_error = 0, initial_counts = [990, 10, 0], final_counts = [190, 63, 747], peak_abm = 188, peak_ode = 158.5, largest_gap = 31) ``` ::: ::: This realization peaks at 188 infectious where the ODE peaks at 158.5, about 19% higher and 0.9 days earlier, and the largest gap between the two curves is 31 individuals. One path is not the mean. To compare levels rather than a single random path, run a small ensemble of seeded replicates. The runs stay stochastic; the seeds only make them reproducible, and the model constructor gives each replicate its own random stream. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-ensemble .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function simulate_abm(seed) model = initialize_model(seed) _, data = run!( model, nsteps; mdata = [susceptible_count, infected_count, recovered_count], showprogress = false, ) return Matrix(data[:, [ :susceptible_count, :infected_count, :recovered_count, ]])' end abm_ensemble = cat((simulate_abm(4000 + k) for k in 1:16)...; dims = 3) abm_mean = dropdims(mean(abm_ensemble; dims = 3), dims = 3) infectious_rmse = sqrt(mean((abm_mean[2, :] .- ode_states[2, :]).^2)) @assert maximum(abs.(sum(abm_ensemble; dims = 1) .- N)) == 0 infectious_rmse ``` ::: {#code-ch06-ensemble .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 6.252915150099244 ``` ::: ::: The comparison is intentionally modest: 16 paths are enough to reveal the relationship and keep a teaching render quick, but not enough for a narrow confidence interval. The ensemble mean is not the same object as the ODE solution, and neither adjustment closes the gap on its own. At fixed $N$, adding replicates shrinks the Monte Carlo error but leaves the finite-population effects unchanged. As $\Delta t\to 0$ the frozen-step error vanishes and the stepped ABM converges to the continuous-time stochastic process for that same finite population. Its ensemble mean converges to that process's expected trajectory, which is generally not the ODE; recovering the ODE also requires a large-population limit. Individual epidemics take off at random times, so their peaks are spread over several time units. Averaging at fixed clock time therefore lowers the peak of the mean curve relative to the mean of the individual pathwise peaks: $$ \max_t \bar I(t) \le \overline{\max_t I(t)}. $$ That orders the two summaries, not the mean curve against every path: a replicate that fades out early can peak below the mean curve. Averaging is not interchangeable with taking a maximum, which Exercise 2 makes quantitative. ## Interpretation and limitations The ABM can be extended by replacing the no-space model with a grid, network, or continuous space, or by adding age, behavior, vaccination, or household fields to `Person`. Those extensions change who can contact whom and can create clustering, superspreading, and spatial waves that a mass-action ODE cannot represent. The price is computational and inferential: agent rules need careful calibration, contact mechanisms can be difficult to observe, and random seeds do not remove structural uncertainty. Our synchronous two-phase update avoids an order artifact. The contact rule samples with replacement, so an agent can draw itself as a contact. A susceptible cannot infect itself, so that draw changes nothing, and keeping it in the pool is what makes the chance of drawing an infectious contact exactly $I_t/N$, the value used in Equation @eq-abm-infection. Excluding it would give $I_t/(N-1)$ instead. A network model would replace this convention with explicit contact constraints. The model is also discrete in time, so $\Delta t$ should be reduced and results checked for timestep sensitivity. Agents.jl's [agent definition documentation](https://juliadynamics.github.io/Agents.jl/v7.0.3/agents/) and [data collection documentation](https://juliadynamics.github.io/Agents.jl/v7.0.3/data/) describe the v7 `@agent`, `StandardABM`, and `run!` APIs. The framework and its modeling rationale are described by Datseris, Vahdati, and DuBois [@datseris2022]. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch08-ex1} Replace the no-space model with a spatial one, so that a susceptible can only contact its immediate neighbors. Use this specification, which keeps the population identical to the chapter's and leaves no ambiguity about who is adjacent to whom: - a periodic $40\times25$ `GridSpaceSingle` with `metric = :chebyshev`, so radius 1 is the eight-cell Moore neighborhood; - one stationary agent per cell, giving $N=1000$ as before; - 10 initial infectives chosen uniformly at random, everyone else susceptible; - the same $\beta$, $c$, $\gamma$, and $\Delta t$; - contacts drawn uniformly from `nearby_agents(person, model, 1)`; - a run of at least 60 time units, continued until $I=0$: spatial spread is far slower than well-mixed spread, and the chapter's 30 units can end while the well-mixed reference and spatial realizations are still running, so a count recorded there need not be a final size. Derive the agent from `GridAgent{2}`, which already supplies `pos`, so do not add a position field by hand. Because the grid is full and periodic, every agent has exactly eight neighbors and the empty-neighborhood case cannot arise. Verify $S+I+R=N$, then compare the final size against the well-mixed model of this chapter over several seeds, using the same stopping rule. Explain which assumption behind Equation @eq-abm-infection has failed. Note that while $\beta$, $c$, and $\gamma$ are unchanged, the combination $\beta c/\gamma=2$ is the *mass-action* reproduction number and is not the spatial model's $R_0$; part of the exercise is to say why not. Repeating the run at radius 5 will help you check your explanation. Confirm that $I=0$ at the end of every run before calling the recovered count a final size; extend the horizon if necessary. ### Exercise 2 {#ch08-ex2} Run the ABM with $\Delta t=0.2$, $0.1$, and $0.05$, over the same physical time span in each case. For each value, report two different statistics of the infectious peak: 1. the peak of the ensemble-mean trajectory, $\max_t \bar I(t)$; and 2. the mean and standard deviation of the per-replicate peaks, $\overline{\max_t I(t)}$. Choose the stopping rule before you name either number a peak. At $t=30$ the epidemic is still going, with the ODE holding about 57.7 infectious, so a maximum recorded by then may well be the eventual peak, but nothing in the run so far establishes that: the path can still climb after the horizon ends, and so can the ensemble-mean curve. To report full-epidemic peaks, run every replicate for at least 30 time units and carry on until $I=0$. Cap the number of steps and raise an error if the cap is ever reached, so that a run which fails to finish is reported rather than cut short in silence. Replicates then stop at different times, so pad the finished trajectories with $I=0$ onto a common time grid before averaging them. If you stop at 30 instead, report both numbers as window maxima over $0\le t\le 30$ and name them that way, not as full-epidemic peaks. The deterministic ODE has $R_0=2$, $I_\text{peak}\approx158.5$ at $t\approx17.5$. Compare both statistics with that value, report whether each lies above or below it, and explain the differences you find. The inequality above orders the two stochastic summaries against each other; it says nothing about where either one sits relative to the ODE, so that has to come from your numbers. One part of each difference can be pinned down. Build the frozen-step mean-field map: apply the ABM's own per-step probabilities to deterministic mean-field counts, holding the infection probability at its start-of-step value for the whole step. This map is not the exact expectation of the ABM, so be careful about what it does and does not establish. The gap between its peak and the ODE peak isolates the frozen-step discrepancy, measured inside the mean-field approximation. The gap that remains between the ABM and the map holds everything else: the finite population, the spread of peak times across replicates, stochastic maximization (taking a maximum along a noisy path pulls the result upward), and whatever interactions those have with the timestep. Report a standard error for *both* estimates. These need different methods: the per-replicate peaks are independent draws, so their mean has the usual $\mathrm{sd}/\sqrt{n}$ standard error, but the peak of the ensemble mean is a maximum taken over an averaged curve, and that same $\mathrm{sd}/\sqrt{n}$ formula does not apply to it. Resample whole replicate trajectories with replacement instead, and recompute the peak on each bootstrap sample. In an initial 64-replicate batch, the standard deviation of the per-replicate peaks was about 24 to 30 people across the three timesteps. With 16 replicates that is a standard error of roughly 6 to 7.5 people on a single mean. Comparing two timesteps is coarser still: the standard error of the difference is about 8.6 to 9.7 people for those same three standard deviations, which cannot settle a gap of a few people either way. Treat 16 as a quick exploratory minimum. To plan a longer run, work backwards from the half-width you are willing to accept. The number of independent replicates each timestep needs is roughly $$ n\approx 2\left(\frac{1.96\,\sigma}{h}\right)^2, $$ where $\sigma$ is the standard deviation of the per-replicate peaks and $h$ is the half-width you want for the approximate 95% confidence interval of the difference. The factor of two is there because both estimates carry error. The formula assumes the same number of replicates at each timestep and one $\sigma$ standing in for both, so it is a planning tool rather than an analysis of the runs you end up with. Taking $\sigma=30$ as a cautious planning value, $h=5$ people needs about 280 replicates per timestep and $h=2$ about 1730. Treat those two counts as starting estimates rather than fixed budgets. The value of $\sigma$ depends on the timestep and on the population size, so run a first batch, measure $\sigma$ from it, and put your own value back into the formula before committing to a long run. Reusing the same seeds across timesteps allows a paired comparison instead, which is cheaper only if the paired peak differences turn out to vary less than the peaks themselves. Two timesteps consume random numbers in different orders, so that correlation is not guaranteed. Measure the standard deviation of the paired differences on a first batch of runs and use it in place of $\sigma$ above, dropping the factor of two. That factor is not needed here because the paired differences already carry the variation from both simulations, so it would count it twice. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/08-agent-based-models.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/08-agent-based-models.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/08-agent-based-models.jl)
